sections.keyIdea: Underemployment is working less, or below your skills, when you want more work — and because it is still work, it changes no unemployment figure at all.

body.text: The specification asks for the **distinction between unemployment and underemployment**, and the distinction is sharp because the measurement is.

items: **Unemployed** — no paid work, available, and actively seeking. Counted as unemployed.
**Underemployed** — in paid work, and wanting more of it or work that uses more of their skills. Counted as **employed**.

body.text: Underemployment takes two forms: working **fewer hours** than wanted, and working in a job that uses **less skill or qualification** than the worker has. Both are a shortfall against what the person could do.

In Andara, 0.9m of the 11.4m employed work part-time and want full-time work. Every one of them has paid work, so every one is counted as employed. The unemployment rate is 5% with them in the figures and 5% without them.

That is why underemployment is measured **separately**. An economy where unemployment is low and underemployment is high has a labour market in worse condition than the unemployment rate alone suggests, and no unemployment figure can show it. It is a genuine waste of resources that the headline measure is not built to see.

realExample.text: A qualified engineer working part-time in a shop while looking for engineering work is employed on every measure, and the skills are idle just the same.

sections.misconception: Students expect underemployment to raise the unemployment rate. It cannot: underemployed people have paid work, so they are employed. Underemployment is a separate measure, which is exactly why it is collected.
sections.examMatters: An Explain (4 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) of a distinction requires both terms and why they are separated. The reason is that the unemployment rate cannot capture underemployment, so the two measures together say more than either alone.

recall.prompt: Complete why underemployment moves no unemployment figure:
template: An underemployed person is in paid ___
so the ILO definition counts them as ___
and Andara's unemployment rate stays at ___
hints: the thing they have some of, and want more of
the group with any paid work at all
unchanged by the 0.9m entirely

sections.title: Employment, Unemployment and Inactivity Rates
sections.keyIdea: The unemployment rate is measured against the labour force and the employment and inactivity rates against the whole working-age population, so the three do not add to 100.

body.text: The specification asks for the **significance of changes in rates of employment, unemployment and economic inactivity**, and the first thing to get right is what each is divided by.

Andara's working-age population is 16m: 11.4m employed, 0.6m unemployed and 4m economically inactive. The **labour force** is the employed plus the unemployed — 12m — and excludes the inactive entirely.

items: **Unemployment rate** = 0.6 ÷ 12 × 100 = **5%** — against the **labour force**.
**Employment rate** = 11.4 ÷ 16 × 100 = **71.25%** — against the **working-age population**.
**Inactivity rate** = 4 ÷ 16 × 100 = **25%** — against the **working-age population**.

body.text: Because the denominators differ, the three rates do **not** add to 100, and none of them can be worked out from the others alone.

The significance is that the unemployment rate can move for reasons that are not about jobs. If unemployed people **stop looking**, they leave the labour force and become inactive: the unemployment rate **falls** and not one extra person is in work. Reading the employment and inactivity rates alongside it is the only way to tell that apart from a genuine improvement.

realExample.text: An unemployment rate falls over a year in which employment did not rise. The people missing from the numerator moved into inactivity, not into jobs.

sections.misconception: Students add the three rates and expect 100. The unemployment rate is measured against the labour force and the other two against the whole working-age population, so the sum has no meaning.
sections.examMatters: A Calculate (2 or 4 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires a calculation from given data with workings shown. Write the denominator down before dividing; the commonest error in this topic is dividing the unemployed by the working-age population.

recall.prompt: Match each rate to the figure it is measured against:

pairs.right: the labour force, 12m
pairs.why: Only people in the labour market can be unemployed within it

pairs.right: the working-age population, 16m
pairs.why: The employment rate asks what share of everyone of working age is in work

pairs.right: the working-age population, 16m, counting those outside the labour force
pairs.why: The inactive are outside the labour force, so the labour force cannot be the denominator

distractors: the total population of the country

sections.title: Net Migration
sections.keyIdea: Net migration changes the labour force and employment at the same time, so employment can rise and the unemployment rate rise with it.

body.text: The specification asks for the **significance of net migration for employment and unemployment** — one requirement covering both, because migration moves the numerator and the denominator together.
Suppose 0.2m people of working age arrive in Andara over a year. 0.15m of them look for work, so they join the labour force; 0.12m find it within the year.

items: **Working-age population**: 16m → 16.2m.
**Labour force**: 12m → 12.15m.
**Employed**: 11.4m → 11.52m — more people in work than before.
**Unemployment rate**: 5% → 5.2% — higher than before.

body.text: Both statements describe the same year. Employment rose and the unemployment rate rose, because the labour force grew faster than employment did. Neither figure is misleading; they answer different questions.

Over a longer period the arithmetic is not the whole story. Arrivals **spend** as well as work, which raises aggregate demand and the labour firms need; they may fill shortages that were holding output back; and where their skills match what employers want, the effect on unemployment is smaller than a one-year snapshot suggests.

realExample.text: An economy takes in workers over a year in which employment grows. Its unemployment rate is higher at the end than at the start, and more people are working than ever.

sections.misconception: Students say that migration raises unemployment. It raises the labour force and usually raises employment too; whether the RATE rises depends on which grows faster, and over time arrivals add to demand as well as to supply.
sections.examMatters: A Discuss (14 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires an argument supported by reasoning, with different viewpoints recognised. The one-year arithmetic and the longer-run demand effect are two such viewpoints, and a good answer holds both.

recall.prompt: Put these steps in the order they follow from arrivals to the unemployment rate, from the migration itself to the effect on the rate:
correctOrder: People of working age arrive: 0.2m of them
Some look for work and join the labour force: 0.15m
Fewer find work within the year: 0.12m
The labour force grew faster than employment, so the rate rises to 5.2%
why: Arrival is the event; nothing in the chain caused it
Only those seeking work enter the labour force, which is the denominator
Employment is the part of the labour force that found a job
The rate depends on which of the two grew faster, not on either alone

takeaway: Without a job, available to start, actively seeking — all three at once.
The underemployed have paid work, so they are employed and move no rate.
Unemployment 5% against the labour force; employment 71.25% against the working-age population.
Employment and the unemployment rate can rise in the same year.

content.title: Causes of Unemployment
content.keyIdea: Five causes, and the evidence that identifies each is different — which matters because what would remove one will not remove another.

sections.title: Frictional Unemployment
sections.keyIdea: Frictional unemployment is the time between leaving one job and starting another, and it exists in every economy including a fully healthy one.

body.text: **Frictional unemployment** is the unemployment that exists because matching a worker to a job takes time. The jobs exist and the workers exist; they have not yet found one another.

items: Someone who has left a job and is looking for a better one.
Someone entering the labour market for the first time after finishing education.
Someone returning after a period away from work.

body.text: It is **short-term and voluntary in character**, and it resolves on its own as the match is made. An economy with none at all would be one in which nobody ever changed job — which would be worse, not better, because moving to a job that suits you better is how output per worker rises.

What changes the amount of it is how easily information moves. Better job information, simpler applications and more effective matching all shorten the gap. A generous system of support during the gap can lengthen it, because it makes waiting for a better match affordable — which is not automatically a bad outcome if the match is better.
It is the benign case. A question asking whether unemployment is a problem should separate this from the three that follow, because the answer for this one is largely no.

realExample.text: A worker leaves one job on Friday and starts another six weeks later. For those six weeks they are unemployed on every measure, and nothing in the economy has gone wrong.

sections.misconception: Students treat all unemployment as a failure. Frictional unemployment is the cost of having a labour market in which people can move, and an economy with none would be one where nobody ever changed jobs.
sections.examMatters: An Explain (4 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires understanding applied to a context. Naming the type is knowledge; saying what the evidence in the extract shows — the length of the spell, whether jobs are available — is the application.

recall.prompt: Complete what frictional unemployment is and is not:
template: Frictional unemployment is the time taken to ___ a worker to a job
so the jobs and the workers both ___
and it tends to be ___ in duration
hints: what a labour market does between the two sides
neither side is missing here
it resolves once the pairing is made

sections.title: Seasonal Unemployment
sections.keyIdea: Seasonal unemployment follows the yearly cycle of the work itself, so it is predictable, repeats, and disappears when the season returns.

body.text: **Seasonal unemployment** happens because the demand for certain work runs on a **yearly cycle**. The work is not there in the off-season, and it returns on schedule.

items: **Agriculture** — labour is needed at planting and harvest and not between them.
**Tourism** — resorts employ heavily in season and very little outside it.
**Construction** — work that depends on the weather stops in the months that do not allow it.

body.text: It differs from frictional unemployment in being **predictable and recurring**. Everyone concerned knows roughly when it starts and when it ends, which is why it is the one type that can be planned for by workers, firms and governments alike.

Because it repeats on a known cycle, unemployment figures are usually published **seasonally adjusted**: the regular yearly pattern is taken out so that a change can be read as a real change rather than as the arrival of a season. Comparing an unadjusted figure with the same month a year earlier does the same job more crudely.

It becomes a serious problem only where a region depends heavily on one seasonal industry, so that the off-season is an annual fall in income for the whole area rather than for a few workers within a varied economy.

realExample.text: A coastal town employs thousands through the summer and a fraction of that through the winter. The pattern is the same every year and everyone plans around it.

sections.misconception: Students read a rise in unemployment between two months as a worsening economy. Much of a month-to-month change is the season arriving, which is why figures are seasonally adjusted before they are compared.
sections.examMatters: An Analyse (6 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires a developed chain. Using a seasonally adjusted figure, or comparing with the same month a year earlier, is the step that makes a claim about a change defensible.

recall.prompt: Sort each spell of unemployment into whether it is frictional or seasonal:

groups.name: Frictional
groups.why: The gap is the time taken to match a worker to a job that already exists
items: A graduate applying for first jobs
A worker who left one job and is choosing between offers

groups.name: Seasonal
groups.why: The work itself runs on a yearly cycle and returns on schedule
items: A fruit picker between harvests
A ski instructor in the summer
A builder in the months that stop outdoor work

sections.title: Structural Unemployment
sections.keyIdea: Structural unemployment is a mismatch between the skills or location of workers and the jobs that exist, so it persists even when there are vacancies to fill.

body.text: **Structural unemployment** is caused by a **mismatch**. There are jobs and there are workers, and the workers cannot take the jobs — because they lack the skills, or because the jobs are somewhere else.

items: **Occupational immobility** — the worker's skills are not the skills the available jobs need, and acquiring new ones takes years.
**Geographical immobility** — the jobs are in another region, and housing costs, family ties or the cost of moving prevent it.

body.text: It is caused by **change in the structure of the economy**: an industry declines, a technology replaces a set of tasks, or production moves abroad. The jobs that go do not return, and the jobs that appear ask for something different.

This makes it the **long-lasting** type, and the one where the damage compounds. Skills decay; the longer someone is out of work the harder work becomes to get; and where an industry was concentrated, a whole region can carry it for a generation.

It is also the type that vacancies cannot fix. An economy can have high structural unemployment and unfilled jobs at the same time, which is the clearest evidence that the problem is the mismatch rather than a shortage of demand.

realExample.text: An industry that employed most of a region closes over a decade. New jobs appear elsewhere in the country and ask for skills the region's workers were never trained in.

sections.misconception: Students treat structural unemployment as a shortage of jobs. The jobs may exist in numbers; they ask for different skills or sit elsewhere. That is why raising demand alone does not remove it.
sections.examMatters: An Examine (8 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires a chain of reasoning, the data given to be interpreted, and a brief assessment of the arguments — the lowest tariff here that asks for evaluation. The relationship between unemployment and unfilled vacancies is the one that identifies a structural cause, and an extract giving both is asking for exactly that inference.

recall.prompt: Put these stages in the order in which structural unemployment develops, from the change in the economy to the lasting effect:
correctOrder: An industry declines or its production moves elsewhere
The jobs it provided disappear and do not return
Different skills, or a different region, are what the new jobs ask for
Workers stay unemployed although vacancies exist
why: The change in the structure of the economy is what starts it
A decline that reversed would leave frictional unemployment, not structural
The mismatch is created here: it is about what the new jobs ask for
Unemployment alongside unfilled vacancies is the signature of a mismatch

sections.title: Demand-Deficiency Unemployment
sections.keyIdea: Demand-deficiency unemployment comes from too little aggregate demand across the whole economy, so it affects every industry at once and rises in a downturn.

body.text: **Demand-deficiency unemployment** is caused by a shortage of **aggregate demand** — total spending across the whole economy — rather than by anything about particular workers or particular industries.

steps.title: Aggregate demand falls
steps.subtitle: households and firms across the economy spend less

steps.title: Firms cannot sell what they produce
steps.subtitle: orders fall and stock builds up

steps.title: Firms cut production
steps.subtitle: because there is no point making what will not sell

steps.title: Workers are laid off across industries
steps.subtitle: and their lost income cuts spending further

body.result: The cause is economy-wide, so the unemployment appears everywhere at once

body.text: Two features identify it. It is **general** — unemployment rises across industries that have nothing in common, which no mismatch could produce. And it moves **with the economy**: it rises through a downturn and falls as output recovers.
Andara's year 3 is the setting for it. Real output fell −2.5% across two consecutive quarters of negative growth, and unemployment caused by that fall is demand-deficiency unemployment by definition.

The last step of the chain is what makes it dangerous: workers who lose income spend less, which reduces aggregate demand further. Unlike frictional unemployment, it does not resolve itself simply by waiting.

realExample.text: Spending falls across an economy at once. Manufacturers, shops and service firms with no supplier in common all cut staff in the same quarter.

sections.misconception: Students explain demand-deficiency unemployment by saying a firm did badly. The cause is a fall in spending across the whole economy, which is why it shows up in industries that have nothing to do with one another.
sections.examMatters: An Evaluate (20 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires arguments weighed and a supported judgement. Which cause of unemployment an economy faces changes what would remove it, so identifying the cause from the data is where such an answer has to start.

recall.prompt: Put these stages in the causal order that runs from falling spending to workers losing jobs, from the first cause to the final effect:
correctOrder: Aggregate demand falls across the whole economy
Firms find they cannot sell everything they produce
Production is cut back, because output that will not sell is not worth making
Workers are laid off across unrelated industries
why: The fall in total spending is the economy-wide change that starts it
Unsold output is how a demand shortage first reaches a firm
Cutting production is the decision that turns unsold stock into fewer jobs
Unemployment across unrelated industries is what identifies the cause as general

sections.title: Real-Wage Inflexibility
sections.keyIdea: Real-wage unemployment exists where wages are held above the level at which everyone willing to work would be hired, so firms want fewer workers than are offering themselves.

body.text: The fifth cause the specification names is **real wage inflexibility**: the case where the wage itself, rather than a shortage of demand or a mismatch of skills, leaves people without work.

At a higher real wage firms want **fewer** workers, because each must produce enough to cover the cost of employing them, and **more** people want to work. If the wage cannot fall, those two quantities need not meet.

On a labour-market diagram, a wage floor above the level at which the two are equal leaves firms wanting 11.2m workers while 11.8m want to work at that wage. The gap of **0.6m** is unemployment caused by the wage, not by the workers.
Wages are held up by a minimum wage set above that level, by collectively agreed pay, by contracts fixed in money terms, and by a reluctance to cut money wages that means firms cut staff instead.

It is the most **contested** of the five, and the disagreement is worth stating rather than resolving. Wages above that level may raise output per worker, and cutting them lowers the income of those who do most of the spending. That the mechanism exists does not settle how much unemployment it explains.

realExample.text: A wage floor is set above the level at which everyone willing to work would be hired. Some workers earn more than they otherwise would, and fewer are employed than at the lower wage.

sections.misconception: Students dismiss this cause by saying that cutting wages would make workers poorer. That is an argument about removing the floor, not a reason the mechanism does not operate. Both belong in an answer.
sections.examMatters: A Discuss (14 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires different viewpoints recognised. This is the clearest case in the topic: the mechanism is straightforward and what follows from it is disputed, and an answer that gives only one side has left out what the command word asks for.

recall.prompt: Match each cause of unemployment to the evidence that would identify it:

pairs.right: short spells, and jobs available to move into
pairs.why: A short gap with jobs available is a matching delay, not a shortage

pairs.right: long spells alongside unfilled vacancies needing other skills
pairs.why: Vacancies that go unfilled while people are unemployed prove a mismatch

pairs.right: unemployment rising across unrelated industries at once
pairs.why: A cause common to unrelated industries has to be economy-wide

pairs.right: more people wanting work at the going wage than firms will hire
pairs.why: A gap at a wage that will not fall points at the wage rather than at demand

takeaway: Frictional and seasonal resolve on their own; the other three do not.
Structural unemployment sits alongside unfilled vacancies, which is how you spot it.
Demand deficiency appears across unrelated industries at once.
A wage floor above the clearing level left 0.6m unemployed in the diagram.

content.title: Effects of Unemployment
content.keyIdea: Six groups, and the two most often missed are the ones that state the cost as lost output rather than lost income.

sections.title: Effects on Consumers and Workers
sections.keyIdea: Unemployment removes income from the people it affects and lowers spending by those still in work, and its cost to a worker outlasts the spell itself.

body.text: Consumers

items: **Lost income for those affected**, so their spending falls immediately and sharply.
**Caution among those still in work.** The fear of losing a job changes what people buy even when their income has not changed, so consumer spending falls by more than the lost wages alone.
**Less spending means fewer sales**, which is how one firm's redundancies reach another firm's order book.

body.text: Workers

The cost to the worker has an immediate part and a lasting one. The immediate part is the lost income. The lasting part is that **skills decay** while unused, and the longer the spell the harder the next job is to get — so a long spell of unemployment lowers a worker's earnings for years after it ends.

items: **Bargaining position weakens**, because a worker who has been out of work accepts less.
**The effect is unequal.** Those with fewer qualifications and less recent experience are unemployed longer.
**The damage outlasts the recovery**, which is why unemployment is treated as more serious than the same fall in output spread evenly.

realExample.text: A worker out of work for a year takes a job below their previous level and earns less than they did for years afterwards. The spell ended; the cost of it did not.

sections.misconception: Students count the cost of unemployment as the wages lost during it. The lasting damage — skills that decayed, the weaker position on returning, lower earnings for years — is usually larger than the income lost in the spell itself.
sections.examMatters: An Analyse (6 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires a developed chain. Lost income, lower spending, fewer sales elsewhere and further job losses is the chain; naming the groups affected is not.

recall.prompt: Complete why unemployment costs more than the wages lost during it:
template: Skills ___ while they are not being used
so the longer the spell the harder the next job is to ___
and earnings stay lower for ___ after the spell ends
hints: what happens to an unused ability over time
the outcome an application is aiming at
the damage outlasts the unemployment by a long way

sections.title: Effects on Firms
sections.keyIdea: Unemployment gives firms a smaller market to sell into and cheaper, more available labour to hire from, so the effect on any one firm depends on which matters more to it.

body.text: Firms are the one group in the specification's list for whom unemployment cuts **both ways**, and saying so is the analysis.
Against the firm

items: **A smaller market.** Unemployed households spend less, and employed households spend cautiously, so sales fall.
**Falling demand hits some firms hardest.** Firms selling goods buyers can postpone — cars, furniture, holidays — lose most.
**Investment is harder to justify** when the market is shrinking, so capacity is not added.

body.text: For the firm

items: **Labour is easier to find.** More applicants for each vacancy, and a better chance of finding the right one.
**Wage pressure is weaker**, so the cost of employing each worker rises more slowly.
**Turnover falls**, because workers are less willing to leave a job when others are scarce.

body.text: Which side dominates depends on the firm. For most, the lost sales outweigh the cheaper labour: a firm cannot be saved by low wages if there is nobody to sell to. For a firm whose costs are mostly labour and whose market is holding up, the balance can go the other way.

realExample.text: A firm hiring during a downturn finds far more applicants for each post, and its sales figures fall in the same quarter.

sections.misconception: Students say unemployment is simply bad for firms. It also delivers cheaper and more available labour. The answer is which effect is larger for the firm in question, which is a judgement to be made from the evidence given.
sections.examMatters: An Examine (8 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires a chain of reasoning, the data given to be interpreted, and a brief assessment of the arguments — the lowest tariff here that asks for evaluation. Unemployment and firms is a relationship with effects in both directions, which is why it suits that command word.

recall.prompt: Sort each consequence of high unemployment into whether it works against a firm or for it:

groups.name: Against the firm
groups.why: These reduce what the firm can sell
items: Households have less income to spend
Buyers postpone purchases they can put off

groups.name: For the firm
groups.why: These reduce what the firm has to pay or makes hiring easier
items: More applicants for each vacancy
Weaker pressure to raise wages
Fewer workers leaving for other jobs

sections.title: Effects on Public Finances
sections.keyIdea: Unemployment hits public finances from both sides at once: less is collected in tax and more is paid out in support, from the same budget.

body.text: The specification names **public finances** as one of the six groups, and the reason it is listed separately is that unemployment moves both sides of the account in the wrong direction at the same time.
Less collected

items: **Income tax** falls, because fewer people are earning.
**Taxes on spending** fall, because households with less income buy less.
**Taxes on profits** fall, because firms selling into a weaker market earn less.

body.text: More paid out

items: **Support for the unemployed** rises directly with the number of people claiming it.
**Other support rises too**, as households on lower incomes qualify for help they did not need before.

body.text: The two together mean the gap between what a government receives and what it spends widens **without any decision having been taken**. Borrowing rises to cover the difference, which raises the interest that must be paid in later years.

There is a further cost that no account records: the **tax that would have been paid** by people who are working, on output that is not being produced. It never appears as a figure and it is larger than the support paid out.

realExample.text: A rise in unemployment widens a government's deficit in the same quarter, without a single change to a tax rate or a spending plan.

sections.misconception: Students count only the support paid to unemployed people. The larger figure is usually the tax no longer collected — income tax, spending taxes and taxes on profits all fall together.
sections.examMatters: An Explain (4 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) of an impact requires a two-stage chain. Fewer people earning, so less income tax collected, so a wider gap between receipts and spending — the middle step is the one most often left out.

recall.prompt: Sort each effect of rising unemployment on public finances into whether it reduces receipts or raises spending:

groups.name: Reduces receipts
groups.why: Less income and less spending in the economy means less tax collected
items: Fewer people paying income tax
Households buying less, so less tax on spending
Firms earning less, so less tax on profits

groups.name: Raises spending
groups.why: More households qualify for support, so more is paid out
items: More people claiming support for the unemployed
More households qualifying for help on low incomes

sections.title: Effects on Resource Utilisation and the PPF
sections.keyIdea: Unemployment means an economy is producing inside its production possibility frontier: the resources exist, the output is possible, and it is not being made.

body.text: The specification names **resource utilisation and the production possibility frontier** as an effect of unemployment, and it is the one that states the cost in terms of output rather than income.

A **production possibility frontier** shows the combinations of goods an economy could produce if all its resources were fully used. A point **on** the frontier uses everything available. A point **inside** it does not.

Unemployment is labour that could be producing and is not, so an economy with unemployed workers is at a point **inside its own frontier**. It is producing less of everything than it could, and the gap between the point and the frontier is output that was possible and was not made.

items: **The frontier has not moved.** Nothing has been destroyed — the workers, the machinery and the materials all still exist.
**The lost output is not recoverable.** A year of output not produced is gone, even though the capacity to produce it remains.
**Long unemployment can move the frontier inward**, because skills decay and machinery left idle is not replaced. A temporary loss becomes a permanent one.

body.text: This is the argument that unemployment is a cost to **everyone** rather than to the unemployed alone. The output that is not made is output nobody consumes.

realExample.text: A factory runs one shift instead of three. The building, the machines and the trained workers all exist, and two shifts of output are simply not produced.

sections.misconception: Students draw unemployment as a frontier shifted inward. The frontier is what the economy COULD produce and it has not moved; unemployment is a point inside it. Only when skills and capital are lost for good does the frontier itself move.
sections.examMatters: A Draw (4 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires an accurately labelled diagram. Both axes labelled with the goods, the frontier drawn and labelled, and the economy marked at a point clearly inside it — not on it and not beyond it.

recall.prompt: Match each position on a production possibility frontier diagram to what it means for an economy:

pairs.right: all available resources are being used
pairs.why: Full utilisation is what the frontier is defined as

pairs.right: resources exist that are not being used
pairs.why: Unemployment puts an economy here: possible output that is not made

pairs.right: not attainable with the resources available
pairs.why: The frontier marks the limit of what the resources allow

pairs.right: the economy can now produce more than before
pairs.why: A change in what is possible is a change in the frontier, not a change in the point

sections.title: Effects on Society
sections.keyIdea: Unemployment carries costs to health, to families and to whole regions that no national accounting figure records, which is why the specification lists society separately.

body.text: The last of the six the specification names is **society**, and it is listed separately because these costs appear in no economic total at all.

items: **Health.** Long unemployment is associated with worse physical and mental health, which raises the cost of healthcare and lowers what people can produce when work returns.
**Families.** Lost income and the strain of insecurity reach everyone in a household, including children whose outcomes are affected for years.
**Regions.** Where unemployment is concentrated, local businesses lose their customers and close, which removes more jobs from the same place.
**Social cohesion.** Areas with sustained high unemployment tend to see more of the problems that follow from lost income and lost routine.

body.text: Two features make these costs distinctive. They are **persistent** — they outlast the unemployment that caused them, sometimes by a generation. And they are **concentrated**, falling on particular places and particular families rather than being spread across a population.

That concentration is the reason a national figure understates them. The same total unemployment spread evenly across a country does far less damage than the same total concentrated in a few regions, and no unemployment rate can tell the two apart.

realExample.text: A town loses its largest employer. Shops, cafés and services that depended on those wages close over the following years, and the town's unemployment outlasts the closure by a generation.

sections.misconception: Students treat social effects as too vague to include. They are the part of the cost that no figure captures, and naming them specifically — health, children's outcomes, regional decline — is what separates an answer that considers them from one that gestures at them.
sections.examMatters: An Evaluate (20 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires arguments weighed and a judgement supported. Costs that no figure records are exactly what a judgement has to weigh, and saying that they are unmeasured is part of weighing them.

recall.prompt: Complete why the social costs of unemployment are understated by a national figure:
template: These costs appear in no economic ___
they ___ the unemployment that caused them
and they are ___ in particular places rather than spread evenly
hints: the kind of figure GDP and the unemployment rate are
they are still there long after the jobs return
a few regions carry most of them

takeaway: The lasting cost to a worker is larger than the income lost during the spell.
For firms it cuts both ways: a smaller market against cheaper, more available labour.
Public finances are hit twice — less tax collected and more support paid.
Unemployment is a point INSIDE the frontier; the frontier itself has not moved.

content.title: The Balance of Payments
content.keyIdea: The current account is one component of the balance of payments and has four lines, so a trade surplus and a current-account deficit can describe the same year.

sections.title: Components of the Balance of Payments
sections.keyIdea: The balance of payments records every transaction between a country and the rest of the world, in three accounts, of which the current account is the one this topic is about.

body.text: The **balance of payments** is the record of all transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a period. The specification asks for its **components, with particular reference to the current account**.

items: **The current account** — trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income.
**The capital account** — transfers of assets between countries, studied in Unit 4.
**The financial account** — purchases and sales of assets across the border, also Unit 4.

body.text: The other two accounts are studied in Unit 4. Knowing that the current account is **one component and not the whole** is what this requirement asks for, and it is the part most often missed.
Inside the current account

items: **Trade in goods** — physical products exported and imported.
**Trade in services** — services sold across borders, such as transport, tourism and financial services.
**Primary income** — income earned from assets abroad, and paid to foreign owners of assets at home.
**Secondary income** — transfers with nothing received in return, such as money sent home by workers abroad.

body.text: Andara's four parts are $18bn, −$6bn, −$9bn and −$5bn, which add to a current account of −$2bn.

realExample.text: A cargo of machinery leaving a port is trade in goods. The insurance sold to the shipping company is trade in services. Both are in the current account and they are not the same line of it.

sections.misconception: Students use "balance of payments" and "current account" as though they meant the same thing. The current account is one of three components, and a question naming one is not asking about the other.
sections.examMatters: A Define (2 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires the meaning of a term. For the balance of payments that is a record of transactions between a country and the rest of the world over a period; naming only trade leaves out most of it.

recall.prompt: Sort each transaction into the part of the current account it is recorded in:

groups.name: Trade in goods
groups.why: A physical product crossing the border
items: Machinery exported to another country
Oil imported from abroad

groups.name: Trade in services
groups.why: A service sold across a border, with nothing physical moving
items: Insurance sold to a foreign shipping company
Spending by foreign tourists

groups.name: Income
groups.why: Money received or paid without a good or service moving in return
items: Profits earned on a factory owned abroad
Money sent home by a worker overseas

sections.title: Trade in Goods and Services
sections.keyIdea: The trade in goods and services balance is exports minus imports of both, and a country can run a surplus on it while the current account as a whole is in deficit.

body.text: The specification asks for the **distinction between deficits and surpluses in the trade in goods and services balance**. It is the two trade lines of the current account added together.

items: **A surplus** — more is earned from exporting goods and services than is spent importing them.
**A deficit** — more is spent importing them than is earned exporting them.

body.text: Andara exported $18bn more in goods than it imported, and spent $6bn more on services than it earned from them. Its trade in goods and services balance is $18bn + −$6bn = **$12bn**, a surplus.

That the two lines can point in opposite directions is the ordinary case rather than an oddity. A country can be a large exporter of goods and a net importer of services, or the other way round, and the balance is the sum of both.

The reason this is distinguished from the current account is coming next: Andara's trade balance is a **surplus of $12bn** and its current account is a **deficit of $2bn**. Both describe the same year and the same country.

realExample.text: A country sells more goods abroad than it buys and pays out more for foreign services than it earns from its own. Its trade balance is the two figures added, not either one of them.

sections.misconception: Students treat the trade balance as the balance of trade in goods alone. The specification names trade in goods AND services, so both lines are in it, and a country whose two lines point in opposite directions is the normal case.
sections.examMatters: A Calculate (2 or 4 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires a calculation from given data with workings shown. Add the goods balance and the services balance, keeping the sign of each; the sign is where this calculation is usually lost.

recall.prompt: Complete the calculation of Andara's trade in goods and services balance:
template: Trade in goods is $18bn and trade in services is ___
adding the two, keeping the sign of each, gives ___
which is a ___
hints: the negative one of the two trade lines
the sum of the two figures above
the word for a positive balance

sections.title: Current Account Deficits and Surpluses
sections.keyIdea: The current account is trade in goods and services plus primary and secondary income, so the income lines can turn a trade surplus into a current-account deficit.

body.text: The specification asks for the **distinction between balance of payments deficits and surpluses on the current account**, and the distinction from the trade balance is where the marks are.
Andara's current account adds four figures: $18bn in goods, −$6bn in services, −$9bn in primary income and −$5bn in secondary income. Together they give **−$2bn** — a deficit.

steps.title: Trade in goods and services: $12bn
steps.subtitle: a surplus, on the two trade lines alone

steps.title: Primary income: −$9bn
steps.subtitle: more paid to foreign owners of assets here than earned on assets abroad

steps.title: Secondary income: −$5bn
steps.subtitle: more transferred out than received

steps.title: Current account: −$2bn
steps.subtitle: the income lines outweigh the trade surplus

body.result: A trade surplus and a current-account deficit, in the same country in the same year

items: **A current account deficit** means more was paid out to the rest of the world than came in, on all four lines.
**A surplus** means the opposite.
**Neither is automatically good or bad.** A deficit means a country is buying more from abroad than it sells there, which can come from strong demand at home as easily as from weak exports.

realExample.text: A country whose industry is largely foreign-owned pays out profits year after year. Its exports can exceed its imports and its current account can still be in deficit.

sections.misconception: Students conclude that a current account deficit means a country is uncompetitive. It can equally mean domestic demand is strong, so imports are high. The deficit is a fact about a balance; what caused it is a separate question the extract has to answer.
sections.examMatters: An Evaluate (20 marks, WEC12 Appendix 6) requires arguments weighed and a judgement supported. Whether a current account deficit matters depends on its size, how long it has lasted and what is behind it, and a judgement that names those conditions is what the command word asks for.

recall.prompt: Put these lines in the order they are added to reach Andara's current account balance, from the trade lines to the final figure:
correctOrder: Trade in goods and services: $12bn
Primary income is added next: −$9bn
Secondary income follows it: −$5bn
All four lines together give −$2bn
why: The two trade lines are added first and give a surplus on their own
Primary income is the first of the two income lines and is negative here
Secondary income is the last line before the total
The total is a deficit, although the trade lines alone were a surplus

takeaway: Three components: current, capital and financial. This topic is the current account.
Trade in goods and services is the two trade lines added, signs kept.
Andara: a trade surplus of $12bn inside a current account deficit of $2bn.
Neither a deficit nor a surplus is automatically good or bad.

notes.title: Measuring National Output
notes.keyIdea: Economic growth is the rate of change of real GDP, and the specification draws three distinctions between measures of GDP and GNI.

items.text: GDP — the total value of goods and services produced inside a country over a period.
GNI — the income received by a country’s residents, wherever in the world it was earned.
Economic growth — the rate of change of real GDP.
Real and nominal — real is at constant prices, nominal at the prices of the year itself. Only real measures output.
Total and per capita — per capita divides by population. Growth equal to population growth leaves it unchanged.
Value and volume — value is in money, volume in quantities. They can move in opposite directions.

takeaway: Real GDP: $500bn → $520bn → $507bn, growth +4% then −2.5%.
Value against volume: +10% volume, −8.3% value, same year.
notes.misconception: A rising nominal GDP is not growth: Andara’s year 3 rose in money and fell in output.

notes.title: Comparing Growth
notes.keyIdea: Comparisons need figures made comparable first, and both a negative growth rate and a recession have exact definitions.

items.text: Between countries — one currency, real figures, per capita where the question is about people.
Over time — one base year, unchanged definitions, equal periods.
PPP — the rate at which a given basket costs the same in both countries.
Negative economic growth — real output smaller than the period before. Not a slower rate.
Recession — two consecutive quarters of negative economic growth.

takeaway: A growth rate falling from 4% to 2% is still growth.
Berewa: $10,000 at the market rate, $20,000 at PPP.
Two negative quarters separated by a positive one is not a recession.
notes.misconception: Subtracting 100 from an index gives the change since the base year, not this year’s inflation.

notes.title: What GDP Leaves Out
notes.keyIdea: GDP counts marketed output, so its limitations are output never counted and things a total cannot show.

items.text: Unpaid work — care, housework, subsistence farming.
Undeclared activity — work deliberately not recorded.
Resources used up — depletion counts as output and never as a loss.
Distribution — the same average, shared evenly or not.
What the output was — repairing damage counts like anything else.
Leisure — the same output in fewer hours is a better outcome and an identical figure.
Indicators — life satisfaction, life expectancy, education, leisure, reported health.
Income and happiness — positive and flattening: extra income adds most where there is least.

takeaway: GDP is a good measure of output and an imperfect proxy for living standards.
Wellbeing indicators ask rather than count, and are used alongside GDP.
The flattening is why GDP per capita tracks wellbeing better in low-income countries.
notes.misconception: "GDP is useless" is a refusal to argue; "imperfect, and here is why" is the argument.

notes.title: Measuring Inflation
notes.keyIdea: A consumer price index is a weighted average over a chosen basket, and every limitation follows from that construction.

items.text: Inflation — a sustained rise in the general price level.
Deflation — a sustained fall in the general price level.
Disinflation — a fall in the rate of inflation, with prices still rising.
Weight each group by its share of spending; multiply weight by price index; add; divide by the total weight.
Andara: 10,580 ÷ 100 = 105.8, so inflation is +5.8%.
Outside the base year, divide by the previous year’s index, not by 100.
An average over one basket: re-weighted to a household spending more on food it was 107.
Fixed between reviews · quality changes hard to price · buyers change what they buy · a sample.
Producer price index — prices at the factory gate, which move before consumer prices do.

takeaway: 105.8 nationally against 107 for a household weighted differently.
Disinflation: prices rising, rate falling. Deflation: index falling.
The producer index rose +11% while the consumer index rose +5.8%.
notes.misconception: Falling inflation is disinflation, and prices are still rising.

notes.title: Causes of Inflation and Deflation
notes.keyIdea: The pair of movements in the price level and real output identifies which cause is operating.

items.text: Demand-pull — AD rises; price level up, real output up.
Cost-push — costs per unit rise, SRAS left; price level up, real output down.
Excessive money growth — the money supply grows faster than output; more money, same goods.
Falling AD — price level down, real output down. Self-reinforcing if buyers wait.
Increase in AS — price level down, real output up.
Fall in the money supply — less to spend, so AD falls and prices with it.

takeaway: Up/up = demand-pull. Up/down = cost-push.
Down/down = falling AD. Down/up = rising AS.
Money growth matters only where it exceeds the growth of output.
notes.misconception: All deflation is not damaging: deflation from rising AS comes with rising output.

notes.title: Effects of Inflation and Deflation
notes.keyIdea: A change in the price level moves real income between groups rather than removing it, and the two directions are not mirror images.

items.text: Consumers — money buys less; under deflation, more, and waiting is rewarded.
The government — receipts rise with inflation and the real debt shrinks; deflation reverses both.
Firms — planning is harder; under deflation revenue falls while money debts do not.
Workers — pay behind prices is a real pay cut; under deflation, pay or jobs are cut.
Income distribution — unexpected inflation moves income from savers and fixed incomes to borrowers.
Investment — discouraged by BOTH, for different reasons.
Competitiveness — turns on inflation relative to trading partners.
The current account — dearer exports and relatively cheaper imports move it towards deficit.

takeaway: $10,000 at 3% became $10,300 and buys what $9,735 bought.
Expected inflation does far less damage than unexpected inflation.
Inflation lower than trading partners’ IMPROVES competitiveness.
notes.misconception: Inflation does not make everyone poorer: a borrower gains what a lender loses.

notes.title: Measuring Employment and Unemployment
notes.keyIdea: The ILO definition decides who is counted; the three rates use two different denominators.

items.text: Without a job · available to start work · actively seeking work. All three at once.
Any paid work makes a person employed. Not seeking or not available makes them inactive.
Unemployment rate = unemployed ÷ labour force = 5%.
Employment rate = employed ÷ working-age population = 71.25%.
Inactivity rate = inactive ÷ working-age population = 25%.
Underemployment — in work and wanting more of it. Counted as employed, so it moves no rate.
Net migration — raises the labour force and employment together; the rate went 5% → 5.2%.

takeaway: The three rates do not add to 100, because the denominators differ.
Unemployed people who stop looking become inactive and the rate falls.
More people in work and a higher unemployment rate can both be true.
notes.misconception: Underemployment cannot raise the unemployment rate: the underemployed have paid work.

notes.title: Causes of Unemployment
notes.keyIdea: Each cause has different evidence behind it, and what removes one will not remove another.

items.text: Frictional — time taken to match a worker to a job. Short; resolves itself.
Seasonal — the work runs on a yearly cycle. Predictable; figures are seasonally adjusted.
Structural — a mismatch of skills or location. Long-lasting; sits beside unfilled vacancies.
Demand deficiency — too little aggregate demand. Appears across unrelated industries at once.
Real wage inflexibility — a wage held above the level at which all willing workers are hired.

takeaway: Unemployment alongside unfilled vacancies means a mismatch, not a shortage of jobs.
A cause common to unrelated industries has to be economy-wide.
At the wage floor: 11.2m wanted, 11.8m willing, 0.6m unemployed.
notes.misconception: Frictional unemployment is not a failure: an economy with none is one where nobody changes jobs.

notes.title: Effects of Unemployment
notes.keyIdea: Unemployment is a loss of output as well as a loss of income, and the costs outlast the spell.

items.text: Consumers — lost income, and caution among those still in work.
Firms — a smaller market against cheaper, more available labour.
Workers — skills decay, and earnings stay lower for years afterwards.
Public finances — less tax collected AND more support paid.
Resource utilisation and the PPF — the economy produces at a point inside its frontier.
Society — health, families and regions; costs no figure records.

takeaway: The frontier has not moved; the economy is at a point inside it.
The tax not collected usually exceeds the support paid out.
Social costs are persistent and concentrated, so a national figure understates them.
notes.misconception: Unemployment does not shift the frontier inward unless skills and capital are lost for good.

notes.title: The Balance of Payments
notes.keyIdea: The current account is one component of the balance of payments and has four lines, so the trade balance and the current account can disagree.

items.text: Current account — trade in goods, trade in services, primary income, secondary income.
Capital account and financial account — named here; studied in Unit 4.
Trade in goods and services = $18bn + −$6bn = $12bn, a surplus.
Current account = that plus −$9bn and −$5bn = −$2bn, a deficit.
A deficit means more paid out than came in. Neither a deficit nor a surplus is automatically good or bad.

takeaway: The current account is not the whole balance of payments.
Keep the sign of each line when adding them.
A trade surplus and a current-account deficit can be the same country in the same year.
notes.misconception: A current account deficit can come from strong demand at home as easily as from weak exports.

quiz.question: Economic growth is measured as the rate of change of:
options: The consumer price index
Nominal GDP
Real GDP
GDP per capita at current prices
quiz.explanation: Growth is defined on real GDP, which is measured at constant prices, so a rise means more output rather than higher prices. A measure at current prices rises whenever prices rise, and the consumer price index measures inflation rather than output.

quiz.question: A country's price index rose by 6% one year and by 2% the next. Over the second year the country experienced:
options: Disinflation
A fall in the price level
No change in prices
Deflation
quiz.explanation: Prices were still rising in the second year and rising more slowly than before, which is disinflation. A fall in the price level would need the index itself to go below the year before, and it did not.

quiz.question: Someone working six hours a week who wants full-time work is counted by the ILO definition as:
options: Outside the working-age population
Unemployed
Economically inactive
Employed
quiz.explanation: Any paid work at all makes a person employed on this definition, however few the hours. Being unemployed requires having no job, and being economically inactive requires not seeking or not being available for work.

quiz.question: Gross National Income differs from Gross Domestic Product in that it measures:
options: Output produced inside the country's borders
Income received by the country's residents
Output valued at constant prices
Income after tax has been deducted
quiz.explanation: GNI draws its boundary around residents and counts the income they receive wherever it was earned, while GDP draws its boundary around the territory and counts output produced inside it. Neither measure is about constant prices or about tax.

quiz.question: Andara's nominal GDP rose from $550.16bn to $552.63bn while its price index rose from 105.8 to 109. Real GDP:
options: Rose to $507bn
Fell to $507bn
Was unchanged at $520bn
Cannot be worked out from this data
quiz.explanation: Dividing the nominal figure by the price index and multiplying by 100 gives $507bn, against $520bn the year before — a fall of −2.5%. The money figure rose because prices rose, which is exactly the situation real GDP exists to reveal.

quiz.question: Andara's real GDP rose +4% in year 2 and its population rose from 25m to 26m. Real GDP per capita:
options: Rose by about 8%
Rose by about 4%
Fell slightly
Was unchanged at $20,000
quiz.explanation: The population rose by the same percentage as output, so output per person was $20,000 before and $20,000 after. Total growth at the rate of population growth leaves living standards, measured this way, exactly where they were.

quiz.question: An exporter shipped 110m barrels at $50 having shipped 100m at $60. Over the year:
options: Volume rose and value fell
Both value and volume rose
Both value and volume fell
Volume fell and value rose
quiz.explanation: Volume is the quantity shipped and it rose +10%. Value is what it earned, and that fell −8.3%, from $6bn to $5.5bn, because the price fell further than the quantity rose.

quiz.question: A recession is defined by the specification as:
options: A fall in the rate of economic growth over two or more quarters
A year in which real GDP falls
Two consecutive quarters of negative economic growth
Any quarter in which unemployment rises
quiz.explanation: The definition counts quarters: two of them, one after the other, each with output smaller than the quarter before. A fall in the rate of growth is not negative growth at all, and an annual figure cannot show whether the quarterly condition was met.

quiz.question: An economy reports growth of 3.0% one year and 1.0% the next. Over the two years its real output:
options: Fell in both of the two years
Fell in the second year and rose in the first
Was larger at the end than at the start
Was unchanged across the two years
quiz.explanation: Both figures are positive, so output rose in both years and is larger at the end than at the start. Growth slowing is a smaller increase, not a decrease; only a negative rate would mean the economy produced less than before.

quiz.question: Berewa's average income converts to $10,000 at the market exchange rate and $20,000 at purchasing power parity. The difference exists because:
options: Berewa's currency buys more at home than the market rate implies
A purchasing power parity always exceeds the market figure
Incomes in Berewa have been rising more quickly
The market exchange rate has been calculated incorrectly
quiz.explanation: A purchasing power parity converts at what money actually buys, and prices for goods and services that cannot be traded across borders tend to be lower in lower-income countries. The market rate is a correct measure of what the currency trades for, which is a different question.

quiz.question: A country's quarterly real growth over a year was +0.4%, −0.9%, −1.4%, −0.6%. The definition of a recession was met:
options: Not at all during the year
At the end of the first quarter
At the end of the second quarter
At the end of the third quarter
quiz.explanation: The first quarter was positive, so the run starts in the second. Two consecutive negative quarters are complete only at the end of the third, which is where the definition is satisfied; the fourth is still negative and still part of the same recession.

quiz.question: Work that was previously done unpaid at home and is now bought from a business will:
options: Reduce measured GDP
Raise measured GDP although the work is the same
Raise GDP only if the business is domestically owned
Leave measured GDP unchanged
quiz.explanation: GDP counts output that passes through a market, so the same work counts once it is paid for and did not count before. That is a limitation of the measure rather than a real increase in what the economy produces.

quiz.question: Which of these is a limitation of GDP that arises because a single total cannot show it, rather than because the output was never counted?
options: Unpaid care given within a family
How evenly income is shared between people
Work paid in cash and not declared
Natural resources used up in production
quiz.explanation: Distribution is invisible in an average: the same GDP per capita can be shared evenly or very unevenly. Unpaid care and undeclared work never enter the accounts at all, and resources used up are output counted with no offsetting loss recorded.

quiz.question: The relationship between real income and reported life satisfaction is best described as:
options: Rising to a peak and then falling once incomes pass a certain level
Showing no relationship at any level of income
Rising at a constant rate across the whole range
Rising steeply at low incomes and flattening as income grows
quiz.explanation: The line rises throughout and flattens, so extra income adds most where there is least of it. It does not turn downward, and a relationship that flattens is not the same as no relationship.

quiz.question: A basket has four groups with weights 30, 25, 20, 25 and price indices 108, 104, 112, 100. The consumer price index is:
quiz.explanation: Multiplying each weight by its index and adding gives 10,580, and dividing by the total weight of 100 gives 105.8. Dividing is what returns the figure to the scale of an index; the undivided total is not one.

quiz.question: A price index moved from 105.8 to 109. Inflation over that year was:
quiz.explanation: Inflation is the change divided by the PREVIOUS year's index: (109 − 105.8) ÷ 105.8 × 100. Subtracting 100 instead gives the change since the base year, which is a different and much larger figure.

quiz.question: Andara's four price changes weighted to a household that spends more of its income on food give an index of 107 rather than 105.8. This shows that:
options: The household is spending more on food than it should
The national index has been calculated incorrectly somewhere in the weighting
A national index is an average that no particular household need experience
Food prices are the only prices that matter to an index
quiz.explanation: Nothing about the prices changed between the two calculations; only the weights did. The national figure is a correct average over average spending, and households weighted differently from the average face something different — here +7% against +5.8%.

quiz.question: The producer price index is watched as an indicator of future consumer price inflation because:
options: Costs reach firms before they reach shops
It is published less often
It is measured more accurately
It covers a wider range of goods
quiz.explanation: A cost has to arrive at a firm before it can be passed into a price on a shelf, so the producer index moves first. It is an indicator rather than a forecast, because a firm may absorb the cost instead of passing it on.

quiz.question: An economy shows a rising price level alongside falling real output. The cause is most likely:
options: An increase in aggregate supply
A fall in aggregate demand
Demand-pull inflation
Cost-push inflation
quiz.explanation: Only a rise in the cost of producing each unit raises the price level while output falls. A rise in aggregate demand would take output up with prices, and both of the other options lower the price level rather than raising it.

quiz.question: Demand-pull inflation on a diagram with the price level and real output on the axes is shown by:
options: Aggregate demand shifting left along an unchanged supply curve
Aggregate demand shifting right along an unchanged supply curve
Short-run aggregate supply shifting left along an unchanged demand curve
Both curves shifting right together
quiz.explanation: Demand-pull starts with a rise in aggregate demand, so that curve moves right and the supply curve stays where it is, taking the price level and real output up together. Supply shifting left is cost-push, and demand shifting left lowers the price level instead.

quiz.question: Growth in the money supply causes inflation when it:
options: Occurs at all
Exceeds the growth of real output
Is decided by a government rather than by banks
Is accompanied by falling unemployment
quiz.explanation: An economy producing more needs more money to buy it, so money growing in line with output raises no prices. It is the excess over what output requires that leaves more money chasing the same quantity of goods.

quiz.question: Prices are falling in an economy whose output is growing. This is caused by:
options: Cost-push inflation
A fall in aggregate demand
A fall in the money supply
An increase in aggregate supply
quiz.explanation: An increase in aggregate supply lowers the price level and raises output at the same time, which is the one combination the other options cannot produce. Both a fall in aggregate demand and a fall in the money supply take output down along with prices.

quiz.question: Deflation caused by falling aggregate demand tends to reinforce itself because:
options: Buyers delay purchases that will be cheaper later
Wages rise faster than prices
The money supply expands automatically
Firms raise prices to protect their revenue
quiz.explanation: If prices are expected to keep falling, waiting is rewarded, and delayed spending is a further fall in aggregate demand. That is what distinguishes this case from deflation caused by rising aggregate supply, where output is rising.

quiz.question: A saver holds $10,000 at 3% interest in a year when inflation is +5.8%. Over the year the saver:
options: Gains, because interest is paid before prices rise
Gains, because the balance is larger
Loses, because the balance buys less than before
Is unaffected, because interest offsets inflation
quiz.explanation: The balance rises to $10,300 and prices rise faster, so it buys what $9,735 bought a year earlier. A larger number of dollars that buys less is a loss, which is why the comparison has to be made in real terms.

quiz.question: Unexpected inflation moves real income towards:
options: Nobody, since everyone loses equally
Savers and away from borrowers
Borrowers and away from savers
Workers and away from firms
quiz.explanation: A debt fixed in money terms is repaid in money that buys less than the money borrowed, so the borrower gains exactly what the lender loses. Inflation moves real income between people rather than removing it from everyone.

quiz.question: Investment tends to fall under both inflation and deflation because:
options: Returns become uncertain under inflation, and waiting is rewarded under deflation
Firms are unable to borrow to fund a project in either case
Governments restrict investment under both inflation and deflation, by law
Interest rates are always high under both inflation and deflation
quiz.explanation: The two work through different mechanisms and point the same way: inflation makes future returns hard to forecast, while deflation makes postponing a project the cheaper decision. That is why the specification lists investment separately from firms.

quiz.question: A country's inflation rate is 5% while its trading partners' is 8%. Its international competitiveness:
options: Is unaffected, because inflation is a purely domestic matter for each country
Worsens, because exports always become dearer
Worsens, because its prices are rising
Improves, because its prices rise more slowly than its partners'
quiz.explanation: Competitiveness depends on inflation relative to trading partners, not on the rate alone. Prices at home are rising and rising more slowly than abroad, so its exports become cheaper in comparison and its current account tends to improve.

quiz.question: Andara has 11.4m employed, 0.6m unemployed and 4m inactive from a working-age population of 16m. The unemployment rate is:
quiz.explanation: The unemployment rate is measured against the labour force, which is the employed plus the unemployed: 0.6 ÷ 12 × 100. Dividing by the working-age population instead gives 3.75%, which is the commonest error in this calculation.

quiz.question: A person must satisfy which conditions to be counted as unemployed on the ILO definition?
options: Without a job and actively seeking work, but availability is not required
Without a job, available to start work, and actively seeking work
Without a job and claiming support from the government
Without a job, and nothing further is required
quiz.explanation: All three conditions must hold at once. Someone without a job who is not available to start, or not looking, is economically inactive rather than unemployed, and the definition makes no reference to claiming support.

quiz.question: 0.2m people of working age arrive in a country over a year. 0.15m join the labour force and 0.12m find work. Over that year:
options: Neither employment nor the rate changed
Employment fell and the unemployment rate rose
Employment rose and the unemployment rate fell
Employment rose and the unemployment rate rose
quiz.explanation: More people are in work at the end than at the start, and the unemployment rate is higher, because the labour force grew faster than employment did — 5% to 5.2%. Both statements describe the same year and answer different questions.

quiz.question: An unemployment rate falls over a year in which employment did not rise. The most likely explanation is that:
options: Some unemployed people stopped looking and became inactive
The working-age population fell over the year
Underemployment increased among those already in work
More of the unemployed found part-time rather than full-time work
quiz.explanation: People who stop seeking work leave the labour force and are counted as economically inactive, which removes them from the numerator of the unemployment rate without putting anyone into work. Underemployment cannot change the rate at all, because the underemployed already have jobs.

quiz.question: An economy has high unemployment and large numbers of unfilled vacancies requiring skills the unemployed do not have. This is:
options: Seasonal unemployment
Demand-deficiency unemployment
Structural unemployment
Frictional unemployment
quiz.explanation: Unemployment sitting alongside vacancies that cannot be filled is a mismatch between the skills or location of workers and the jobs available, which is what structural unemployment means. A shortage of aggregate demand would not leave vacancies unfilled.

quiz.question: Unemployment rises at the same time across manufacturing, retail and services with no supplier in common. This points to:
options: Real-wage inflexibility
Structural unemployment
Demand-deficiency unemployment
Frictional unemployment
quiz.explanation: A cause showing up in industries with nothing in common has to be economy-wide, and a fall in aggregate demand is exactly that. A mismatch of skills would affect particular industries rather than all of them at once.

quiz.question: A worker who has left one job and expects to start another within two months is experiencing:
options: Frictional unemployment
Demand-deficiency unemployment
Structural unemployment
Seasonal unemployment
quiz.explanation: The gap is the time taken to match a worker to a job that already exists, which is frictional and resolves as the match is made. Structural unemployment lasts because the jobs available need something the worker does not have.

quiz.question: A wage floor leaves firms wanting 11.2m workers while 11.8m are willing to work at that wage. The 0.6m difference is unemployment caused by:
options: Workers choosing not to accept the jobs on offer
A shortage of aggregate demand across the economy
A mismatch between workers' skills and the jobs that employers have available
The wage being held above the level that would hire everyone willing
quiz.explanation: At that wage more people offer themselves than firms will hire, and the wage cannot fall to close the gap. The workers are willing to work at the going wage, which is what separates this from a choice not to take a job.

quiz.question: Unemployment figures are usually published seasonally adjusted so that:
options: The published figures look smaller than they really are
A change can be read as a real change rather than the arrival of a season
Frictional unemployment can be excluded from the total before publication
Only full-time work is counted towards the published figure
quiz.explanation: The regular yearly pattern is taken out, so a month-to-month movement reflects something other than the season arriving on schedule. The adjustment changes neither what is counted nor who is included.

quiz.question: On a production possibility frontier diagram, an economy with unemployed workers is shown:
options: On the frontier
Inside the frontier
Beyond the frontier
With the frontier shifted inward
quiz.explanation: The resources still exist, so what the economy could produce has not changed and the frontier stays where it is; the economy is simply producing less than it could, at a point inside it. The frontier itself moves inward only when skills and capital are lost for good.

quiz.question: The effect of rising unemployment on public finances is that:
options: Receipts rise and spending falls
Receipts and spending both fall
Neither is affected until tax rates change
Receipts fall and spending rises
quiz.explanation: Fewer people earning means less income tax, less spending means less tax on spending, and more households qualify for support at the same time. Both sides of the account move in the unhelpful direction without any decision being taken.

quiz.question: High unemployment affects firms in that it:
options: Reduces their sales and lowers their labour costs
Has no effect until wages are renegotiated
Only reduces their sales
Only lowers their labour costs
quiz.explanation: It cuts both ways: households with less income buy less, and at the same time there are more applicants for each vacancy and weaker pressure to raise wages. For most firms the lost sales outweigh the cheaper labour, which is a judgement rather than a definition.

quiz.question: The lasting cost of unemployment to a worker is usually larger than the wages lost during it because:
options: The worker loses their place in the working-age population
Support payments are taxed
Skills decay, so earnings stay lower for years afterwards
Firms are required to rehire at a lower wage
quiz.explanation: Skills that go unused deteriorate and a long spell weakens a worker's position on returning, so earnings remain below what they would have been long after the spell ends. That is why unemployment is treated as worse than the same loss of output spread evenly.

quiz.question: The current account of the balance of payments records:
options: Trade in goods only
Trade in goods and services only
Trade in goods, trade in services, primary income and secondary income
All transactions between a country and the rest of the world, of every kind
quiz.explanation: The current account has four lines, of which trade is two. All transactions between a country and the rest of the world is the balance of payments as a whole, which also contains the capital and financial accounts.

quiz.question: A country's trade in goods balance is $18bn and its trade in services balance is −$6bn. Its trade in goods and services balance is:
options: $12bn
$18bn
−$2bn
$24bn
quiz.explanation: The two lines are added with the sign of each kept: $18bn + −$6bn = $12bn, a surplus. Adding the figures as though both were positive gives $24bn, which is where this calculation is usually lost.

quiz.question: A country has a trade in goods and services surplus of $12bn and a current account deficit of $2bn. This is possible because:
options: The capital account is included in the current account
A surplus and a deficit cannot both occur
One of the two figures must be an error
Primary and secondary income are also in the current account
quiz.explanation: The current account adds primary income of −$9bn and secondary income of −$5bn to the trade lines, and together those outweigh the trade surplus. The capital account is a separate component of the balance of payments.

practice.question: Define the term ‘gross domestic product’ (GDP). (2 marks)
practice.guidance: Define requires the meaning of a term (WEC12 Appendix 6), and it carries 2 marks in IAL Economics. The total value of goods and services produced inside a country over a period of time: the boundary and the period are what make it a definition rather than a description. Nothing else is required — a Define does not ask for the three distinctions between measures, for how the figure is used, or for its limitations.

practice.question: A country’s real GDP was $520bn in year 2 and $507bn in year 3. Calculate its rate of economic growth in year 3. (2 marks)
practice.guidance: Calculate requires a calculation from given data, and workings should be shown (WEC12 Appendix 6). The rate of economic growth is the change in real GDP divided by the earlier figure, multiplied by 100: ($507bn − $520bn) ÷ $520bn × 100 = −2.5%. Divide by the EARLIER figure, not the later one, and keep the sign: it is part of the answer, because it is what says output fell rather than rose.

practice.question: Explain two reasons why a rise in real GDP per capita may not mean that living standards have improved. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Explain requires knowledge and understanding applied to a context, and a two-stage chain where a reason is asked for (WEC12 Appendix 6). Two from: the average says nothing about distribution, so a rise concentrated among a few leaves most people where they were; the output may be spending that repairs damage rather than adding anything; the extra output may have been produced by working longer hours, which is a cost the figure cannot see; and output that depletes a resource counts in full with no loss recorded. Take two and join each to the living standard by a reason. Naming four limitations without joining any of them to living standards answers a different question.

practice.question: A consumer price index is built from four groups with weights of 30, 25, 20, 25 and price indices of 108, 104, 112, 100. Calculate the index and the rate of inflation if the base year index was 100. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Calculate requires a calculation involving several stages, with workings shown (WEC12 Appendix 6). Multiply each weight by its index: 30 × 108 = 3,240; 25 × 104 = 2,600; 20 × 112 = 2,240; 25 × 100 = 2,500. Add them: 10,580. Divide by the total weight of 100: 105.8. Inflation is the percentage change from the base year index of 100, so +5.8%. Set the weighted total, the division and the percentage change out separately, so that a slip in one of them is visible.

practice.question: Draw an accurately labelled aggregate demand and aggregate supply diagram to show the effect of a sharp rise in imported energy costs on the price level and real output. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Draw requires an accurately labelled diagram, using quantitative skills (WEC12 Appendix 6), so the labels are the answer rather than decoration. Required: the price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal, both labelled; a downward-sloping AD and an upward-sloping SRAS₁; a second curve SRAS₂ drawn up and to the LEFT of SRAS₁, since a cost rise means less is supplied at every price level; SRAS₁ kept on the page, because a shift is only visible against where the curve was; an arrow showing the direction; and dashed guides reading off the higher price level and the lower real output. That pairing — price level up, output down — is what identifies the cause as cost-push.

practice.question: Analyse how a rise in a country’s inflation rate relative to its trading partners affects its current account. (6 marks)
practice.guidance: Analyse requires a developed chain of reasoning (WEC12 Appendix 6), so the links matter more than the number of points.
