Prices at home rise faster than abroad; exports therefore become dearer for foreign buyers while imports become relatively cheaper at home; buyers switch, with the size of the switch depending on how easily the goods can be replaced; export earnings fall and import spending rises, so the current account moves towards deficit. Develop one chain properly rather than naming several effects. The first link is the comparison with trading partners: an answer starting from the inflation rate alone reaches a conclusion that is wrong for a country whose partners have higher inflation still.

practice.question: Examine the relationship between the unemployment rate, the employment rate and the economic inactivity rate as measures of the labour market. (8 marks)
practice.guidance: Examine requires knowledge, understanding, application, analysis AND evaluation (WEC12 Appendix 6): an explanation with a chain of reasoning, the data given interpreted, and a brief assessment of the arguments. Set out the measurements first: the unemployment rate is measured against the labour force, the employment and inactivity rates against the whole working-age population, so the three do not sum to 100 and none can be derived from the others. Then consider what the relationship reveals. An unemployment rate falling while the employment rate is flat means people moved from unemployment into inactivity, not into work. A rising inactivity rate can hide a weakening labour market behind an improving unemployment figure. Net migration can raise employment and the unemployment rate together. Conclude on what reading all three allows that reading one does not.

practice.question: Explain two causes of unemployment that would not be removed by a rise in aggregate demand. (4 marks)
practice.guidance: Explain requires a two-stage chain where a reason is asked for (WEC12 Appendix 6). Two from structural, frictional, seasonal and real wage inflexibility, each joined to why extra demand leaves it in place. Structural: the jobs exist already and go unfilled because workers lack the skills or live elsewhere, so more demand adds vacancies of the same kind. Real wage inflexibility: the gap is between the workers firms will hire at a wage that cannot fall and the workers willing at it, so extra demand does not close it while the floor holds. Do not offer demand deficiency — it is the one cause a rise in aggregate demand does remove, which is what the question is contrasting the others with.

practice.question: Discuss the costs of unemployment to an economy. (14 marks)
practice.guidance: Discuss requires an argument supported by a chain of reasoning, with different viewpoints recognised (WEC12 Appendix 6). Build the costs across the groups the specification names: consumers lose income and those still in work spend cautiously; workers suffer skills decay that lowers earnings for years after the spell; public finances lose tax receipts and pay more support at once; the economy produces at a point inside its production possibility frontier, so output that was possible is not made; and society carries health, family and regional costs that no figure records. Then recognise the other viewpoints: some unemployment is frictional and is the cost of a labour market in which people can move; firms gain cheaper and more available labour; and the size of the cost depends on the cause, on how long spells last and on whether unemployment is concentrated in particular regions. Reach a conclusion about which costs dominate for the economy in the question.

practice.question: Evaluate whether a persistent current account deficit should be a matter of concern for a government. (20 marks)
practice.guidance: Evaluate requires arguments to be reviewed and weighed, with a supported judgement (WEC12 Appendix 6). The case for concern: a deficit means more is paid out to the rest of the world than comes in, it has to be financed, and if it reflects a loss of competitiveness from inflation above trading partners it will not close on its own. The case against: a deficit can reflect strong demand at home rather than weak exports; it can reflect investment in imported capital goods that raises future output; and a country whose industry is largely foreign-owned can run a trade surplus and a current account deficit at the same time, as this chapter’s figures do, which says more about ownership than about competitiveness. Weigh the two on nameable conditions: the size of the deficit relative to GDP, how long it has persisted, what is behind it, and how easily it is financed. A judgement that depends on those conditions is what this command word asks for; a judgement that a deficit is simply good or simply bad is not.

flashcards.front: What is GDP?
flashcards.back: The total value of goods and services produced inside a country over a period of time. A flow, not a stock: it counts what was produced, not what is owned.

flashcards.front: What is economic growth?
flashcards.back: The rate of change of real GDP. Not the level of GDP, and not a nominal figure — a measure that rose whenever prices rose could not answer the question growth is asked.

flashcards.front: What is GNI and how does it differ from GDP?
flashcards.back: Gross National Income is income received by a country’s residents, wherever earned. GDP draws its boundary around the territory; GNI around the residents.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between real and nominal GDP?
flashcards.back: Nominal is at the prices of the year itself; real is at the prices of one fixed base year. Only real GDP measures output, because only it holds prices constant.

flashcards.front: Why can real GDP rise while real GDP per capita does not?
flashcards.back: Because the population rose at the same rate. Growth above population growth raises output per person, growth equal to it leaves it unchanged, and growth below it lowers it.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between value and volume?
flashcards.back: Value is measured in money; volume in quantities. They can move in opposite directions — more barrels shipped for less money — so a figure in dollars cannot tell you what happened to output.

flashcards.front: What has to be done before two countries’ growth can be compared?
flashcards.back: Convert to one currency, compare real with real, use per capita figures where the question is about people, and do not mix a growth rate with a level.

flashcards.front: What is a purchasing power parity?
flashcards.back: The conversion rate at which a given basket of goods costs the same in two countries. It compares incomes by what they buy rather than by what the currency trades for.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between negative growth and a falling growth rate?
flashcards.back: Negative growth means real output is smaller than before. A falling rate means output is still larger than before and grew by less than it did.

flashcards.front: What is the definition of a recession?
flashcards.back: Two consecutive quarters of negative economic growth. Two, one after the other, measured quarterly, with output smaller than the quarter before.

flashcards.front: Name the limitations of GDP as a measure of living standards.
flashcards.back: Never counted: unpaid work, undeclared activity, resources used up. A total cannot show: distribution, what the spending was for, leisure.

flashcards.front: What are indicators of national happiness and wellbeing?
flashcards.back: Measures of how life is experienced rather than what is produced: life satisfaction, life expectancy, education, leisure, reported health. Used alongside GDP, and they ask rather than count.

flashcards.front: What is the relationship between real incomes and subjective happiness?
flashcards.back: Positive and flattening. Satisfaction rises with real income everywhere and rises less and less: extra income adds most where there is least of it.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between inflation, deflation and disinflation?
flashcards.back: Inflation — a sustained rise in the general price level. Deflation — a sustained fall in it. Disinflation — a fall in the rate, with prices still rising.

flashcards.front: How is a consumer price index calculated?
flashcards.back: Weight each group by its share of spending, multiply each weight by its price index, add the results, and divide by the total weight. Inflation is then the percentage change in that index.

flashcards.front: What is the commonest error in calculating inflation from an index?
flashcards.back: Subtracting 100 in a year that is not the base year. Divide by the previous year’s index, not by 100 — the two agree only in the base year, which is why the error survives.

flashcards.front: What are the limitations of the CPI?
flashcards.back: It is an average over one basket, so no household need experience it; the basket is fixed between reviews; quality changes are hard to price; buyers change what they buy; and it is a sample.

flashcards.front: What is the producer price index used for?
flashcards.back: As an indicator of future trends in the rate of inflation. It measures prices at the point firms trade, and a cost reaches a firm before it reaches a shelf.

flashcards.front: Name the three causes of inflation.
flashcards.back: Demand-pull — aggregate demand rises. Cost-push — the cost of producing each unit rises. Excessive growth of the money supply — money grows faster than output.

flashcards.front: Name the three causes of deflation.
flashcards.back: Falling aggregate demand; an increase in aggregate supply; a fall in the money supply. Two lower output with prices and one raises it.

flashcards.front: How do you tell demand-pull from cost-push on the data?
flashcards.back: By what real output did. Price level up with output up is demand-pull; price level up with output down is cost-push.

flashcards.front: How do you tell the two kinds of deflation apart?
flashcards.back: Again by real output. Price level down with output down is falling aggregate demand; down with output up is an increase in aggregate supply.

flashcards.front: Name the eight groups affected by inflation and deflation.
flashcards.back: Consumers · the government · firms · workers · income distribution · investment · competitiveness · the current account of the balance of payments.

flashcards.front: Who gains and who loses from unexpected inflation?
flashcards.back: Borrowers gain — a fixed debt is repaid in money worth less. Savers, lenders and fixed incomes lose by the same amount. It moves real income rather than removing it.

flashcards.front: Why does investment fall under both inflation and deflation?
flashcards.back: Under inflation, future returns become uncertain, and uncertainty discourages commitment. Under deflation, waiting is rewarded, so projects are postponed. Different reasons, same direction.

flashcards.front: What is the ILO definition of unemployment?
flashcards.back: Without a job · available to start work · actively seeking work. All three at once. Any paid work makes a person employed; not seeking or not available makes them inactive.

flashcards.front: What is underemployment?
flashcards.back: Being in paid work and wanting more of it, or work that uses more of your skills. The underemployed are counted as employed, so underemployment moves no unemployment rate at all.

flashcards.front: What is each labour-market rate measured against?
flashcards.back: Unemployment rate — against the labour force (employed + unemployed). Employment and inactivity rates — against the working-age population. They do not sum to 100.

flashcards.front: Why can employment and the unemployment rate rise together?
flashcards.back: Because net migration raises the labour force and employment at the same time. If the labour force grows faster than employment does, more people are in work and the rate is higher.

flashcards.front: Name the five causes of unemployment.
flashcards.back: Frictional · seasonal · structural · demand deficiency · real wage inflexibility. The first two resolve on their own; the other three do not.

flashcards.front: How do you identify structural unemployment from data?
flashcards.back: High unemployment sitting alongside unfilled vacancies that need other skills or are in other regions. A shortage of demand would not leave vacancies unfilled.

flashcards.front: How do you identify demand-deficiency unemployment?
flashcards.back: It appears across unrelated industries at once and moves with the economy. A cause common to industries with nothing in common has to be economy-wide.

flashcards.front: What is real wage inflexibility?
flashcards.back: A wage held above the level at which everyone willing to work would be hired, so firms want fewer workers than are offering themselves. The most contested of the five causes.

flashcards.front: Name the six effects of unemployment.
flashcards.back: Consumers · firms · workers · public finances · resource utilisation and the PPF · society. The last two state the cost as lost output rather than lost income.

flashcards.front: Why does unemployment hit public finances twice?
flashcards.back: Less collected — income tax, taxes on spending and taxes on profits all fall. More paid out — support for the unemployed and for households on lower incomes. The gap widens with no decision taken.

flashcards.front: How is unemployment shown on a production possibility frontier?
flashcards.back: As a point inside the frontier. The resources still exist, so the frontier has not moved; the economy is producing less than it could, and that output is not recoverable.

flashcards.front: What are the components of the balance of payments?
flashcards.back: The current account, the capital account and the financial account. The current account is one component, not the whole.

flashcards.front: What is in the current account?
flashcards.back: Trade in goods · trade in services · primary income · secondary income. Trade is two lines of four, which is why a trade surplus and a current account deficit can coexist.

flashcards.front: What is the trade in goods and services balance?
flashcards.back: The goods balance plus the services balance, with the sign of each kept. The two lines often point in opposite directions, and the balance is their sum.

flashcards.front: Is a current account deficit a bad thing?
flashcards.back: Not automatically. It means more was paid out than came in, which can reflect strong demand at home or investment in imported capital as easily as weak exports. What caused it is a separate question.

diagrams.title: Measuring National Output
diagrams.description: Andara's national accounts over three years, with real GDP derived from the nominal figure and the price index, and real GDP per head derived from the population. The three distinctions the specification draws between measures of GDP and GNI — real and nominal, total and per capita, value and volume — all read off these figures.
checklist: Real GDP = nominal GDP ÷ price index × 100, so both are measured at the same prices
Real GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population

diagrams.title: Comparing Growth
diagrams.description: Positive against negative growth rates, the quarterly pattern the specification defines a recession by, and what purchasing power parities change about a comparison between two countries.
checklist: A growth rate is the percentage change in REAL GDP, not in nominal GDP
A negative growth rate means real output fell, not that growth slowed
A recession is two CONSECUTIVE quarters of negative growth
A comparison between countries needs one currency, and the market rate is not the only one
PPP converts at what the money actually buys, which is why it is used for living standards

diagrams.title: Measuring Inflation
diagrams.description: How a consumer price index is built from a weighted basket, what the same price changes do to a household whose spending is weighted differently, the difference between inflation, disinflation and deflation in one series, and why the producer price index is watched as an indicator of future trends.
checklist: Each group carries a weight, and the weights add to the total the index is divided by
Multiply each weight by its price index, add them, divide by the total weight
Inflation is the percentage change in the index, not the level of the index
Disinflation is a fall in the RATE while prices are still rising
Deflation is a fall in the index itself
A national index is an average, so no household need experience it

diagrams.title: Causes of Inflation and Deflation
diagrams.description: Demand-pull and cost-push inflation, and the two causes of deflation the specification names on the demand and supply sides, each drawn on axes of the price level against real output. The price level ends higher in both inflation cases and lower in both deflation cases; what separates them is what happened to output.
checklist: Price level on the vertical axis and real output on the horizontal, both labelled
Aggregate demand sloping down and short-run aggregate supply sloping up
The curve that moved drawn beside the original, never instead of it, and labelled AD₂ or SRAS₂
The old and new price levels read off with dashed guides
Demand-pull: the price level and output both rise
Cost-push: the price level rises and output falls
Falling AD: the price level and output both fall
Rising AS: the price level falls and output rises

diagrams.title: Causes of Unemployment
diagrams.description: The five causes the specification names, each set against what is actually happening and whether it resolves without intervention, and the real-wage case drawn as a labour market with a wage that cannot fall.
checklist: Name the cause from what is happening, not from how long it has lasted
Frictional and seasonal unemployment resolve on their own; the other three need something to change
Structural unemployment is a mismatch of skills or place, not a shortage of jobs in total
Demand-deficiency unemployment is a shortage of demand across the whole economy
Real-wage unemployment is a gap between the workers wanted and the workers willing at a wage that cannot fall

diagrams.title: Effects of Unemployment
diagrams.description: The six groups the specification names, and the production possibility frontier it names alongside them: an economy with unemployed workers produces at a point inside its own frontier, so the loss is output that was possible and was not made.
checklist: A point inside the frontier is unused resources, not a smaller frontier
The CAPACITY is recoverable — the frontier has not moved — but the output not made this year is gone for good
Public finances are hit twice: less tax collected and more support paid
The cost to a worker outlasts the unemployment, because skills decay

chains.title: How a cost travels from a raw material to a shop price
steps: The price of a raw material rises.
The producer price index records higher input prices.
Firms raise the prices of the finished goods they sell on.
The consumer price index records higher prices in shops.
chains.result: The producer index leads the consumer index because a cost reaches a firm before it reaches a shelf

chains.title: How structural unemployment develops
steps: An industry declines or its production moves elsewhere.
The jobs it provided disappear and do not return.
The new jobs appearing need different skills, or are in a different region.
Workers stay unemployed although vacancies exist.
chains.result: Unemployment alongside unfilled vacancies is the signature of a mismatch rather than a shortage of jobs

chains.title: How net migration moves employment and the unemployment rate together
steps: 0.2m people of working age arrive.
0.15m of them look for work and join the labour force, taking it to 12.15m.
0.12m of them find work within the year, taking employment to 11.52m.
The labour force grew faster than employment, so the unemployment rate rises to 5.2%.
chains.result: More people in work and a higher unemployment rate, both true of the same year

chains.title: How a nominal rise can hide a real fall
steps: Prices across the economy rose, taking the index from 105.8 to 109.
The same output would therefore sell for more dollars.
Nominal GDP rose +0.4%, to $552.63bn.
Valued at constant prices, real GDP fell −2.5%, to $507bn.
chains.result: Economic growth is defined on real GDP precisely so that a price rise cannot be read as growth

chains.title: How a weighted basket becomes a rate of inflation
steps: Survey households to find what they spend their money on, and weight each group by its share.
Multiply each weight by its price index: 3,240, 2,600, 2,240, 2,500.
Add them and divide by the total weight: 10,580 ÷ 100 = 105.8.
Take the percentage change from the previous year's index to get inflation of +5.8%.
chains.result: Re-weighted to a household spending more on food the same prices give 107, which is what "an average" means

chains.title: How a trade surplus sits inside a current account deficit
steps: Trade in goods is $18bn and trade in services is −$6bn.
Added with their signs, trade in goods and services is $12bn — a surplus.
Primary income is −$9bn and secondary income is −$5bn.
All four lines together give a current account of −$2bn — a deficit.
chains.result: The income lines outweighed the trade surplus, which is why 4b and 4c are distinguished from one another

mistakes.title: Reading a Nominal Rise as Growth
mistakes.mistake: Students see GDP measured in dollars rise and conclude that the economy grew.
mistakes.correction: A nominal figure rises whenever prices rise, whatever happened to output. Andara's year 3 is the case: nominal GDP rose +0.4% and real GDP fell −2.5%. Economic growth is defined on REAL GDP, at constant prices, precisely so that this cannot happen.
mistakes.examTip: Check which figure the extract gives you. If it is in money and no price index is mentioned, say what would have to be true about prices for the conclusion to hold.

mistakes.title: Treating Total Growth as Rising Living Standards
mistakes.mistake: Students take a growth rate as evidence that people are better off.
mistakes.correction: Total growth has to be set against population growth. Andara's real GDP rose +4% in year 2 and real GDP per capita changed by 0%, because the population rose at the same rate. The economy was larger and the average person was exactly where they started.
mistakes.examTip: Use the per capita figure whenever the question is about living standards, and say so. If the extract gives only the total, say what the population would have to have done.

mistakes.title: Calling Falling Inflation Deflation
mistakes.mistake: Students describe inflation falling from 6% to 2% as deflation.
mistakes.correction: Prices are still rising at 2%, so that is inflation, and the fall in the RATE is disinflation. Deflation requires the index itself to fall below the previous year. Andara's index went 100 → 105.8 → 109: inflation both years, disinflation in the second, deflation in neither.
mistakes.examTip: Look at the index, not the rate. A falling rate with a rising index is disinflation; a falling index is deflation.

mistakes.title: Subtracting 100 From an Index That Is Not the Base Year
mistakes.mistake: Students calculate inflation by taking 100 off whatever index they are given.
mistakes.correction: That gives the change since the BASE year, not the rate over the last one. From 105.8 to 109 the rate is (109 − 105.8) ÷ 105.8 × 100 = +3%, not the +9% that subtracting 100 would give.
mistakes.examTip: Write down which year you are dividing by before you divide. The two methods agree only in the base year, which is why the error survives to the year where it matters.

mistakes.title: Naming a Cause of Inflation Without Using the Output Figure
mistakes.mistake: Students assert that inflation is demand-pull or cost-push from the price data alone.
mistakes.correction: The price level rises in both cases, so the price data cannot separate them. Real output is what does: up with prices is demand-pull, down with prices is cost-push. The same test separates the two deflations — output down is falling aggregate demand, output up is an increase in aggregate supply.
mistakes.examTip: Quote both figures from the extract before naming the cause. A data question that gives an output figure alongside a price figure is asking for exactly that inference.

mistakes.title: Dividing the Unemployed by the Working-Age Population
mistakes.mistake: Students calculate an unemployment rate against the wrong denominator.
mistakes.correction: The unemployment rate is measured against the LABOUR FORCE — the employed plus the unemployed. For Andara that is 0.6 ÷ 12 = 5%. Dividing by the working-age population of 16m gives 3.75%, a different figure for a different question. The employment and inactivity rates DO use the working-age population, which is where the confusion starts.
mistakes.examTip: Write the denominator down before dividing. If the three rates you have calculated add to 100, you have used the same denominator for all three and at least one is wrong.

mistakes.title: Expecting Underemployment to Raise the Unemployment Rate
mistakes.mistake: Students add the underemployed to the unemployed when calculating a rate.
mistakes.correction: Underemployed people have paid work, so the ILO definition counts them as employed. Andara's 0.9m part-time workers wanting full-time work change no rate at all. That is precisely why underemployment is measured separately: the unemployment rate cannot show it.
mistakes.examTip: Say that underemployment leaves the rate unchanged and that this is why it is collected as its own measure. That sentence is the point of the distinction.

mistakes.title: Drawing Unemployment as a Frontier Shifted Inward
mistakes.mistake: Students show unemployment by moving the production possibility frontier itself.
mistakes.correction: The frontier shows what the economy COULD produce, and unemployed workers still exist, so it has not moved. Unemployment is a point INSIDE the frontier: output that is possible and is not being made. Only when skills decay and capital is scrapped for good does the frontier itself move inward.
mistakes.examTip: Mark the economy clearly inside the curve and label the gap. If your diagram has moved the frontier, you have drawn a loss of capacity rather than a failure to use it.

mistakes.title: Treating the Current Account as the Balance of Payments
mistakes.mistake: Students use the two terms as though they were interchangeable.
mistakes.correction: The balance of payments has three components — current, capital and financial — and the current account is one of them, with four lines of its own. A country can run a trade in goods and services surplus of $12bn and a current account deficit of $2bn in the same year, as the chapter's figures do, because primary and secondary income are in the current account too.
mistakes.examTip: Answer about the account the question names. If it says current account, the income lines are in scope; if it says trade balance, they are not.

mistakes.title: Concluding That a Current Account Deficit Means Weak Competitiveness
mistakes.mistake: Students read a deficit as evidence that a country cannot compete.
mistakes.correction: A deficit means more was paid out than came in, and strong demand at home raises imports just as effectively as weak exports do. It can also reflect imported capital goods bought to raise future output, or profits paid to foreign owners of domestic industry, neither of which says anything about competitiveness.
mistakes.examTip: Say what the deficit means, then use the extract to say what caused it. An Evaluate on whether it matters is judged on the size, how long it has lasted and what is behind it.
